Controlling for real GDP growth as a proxy for real disposal income growth and period fixed effects, a 1pp rise in the dependency ratio reduces real private consumption growth by an average of 3bp (Exhibit 4). Korea stands out for the estimated impact of aging on consumption. JPM.title: Brazil : Exposure to Russia’s fuel
JPM.excerpt: …come from Russia (Figures 1 and 2). Currently, around 8.5% of the gasoline consumed in Brazil is imported and around 25% of the diesel is imported. As a result, we estimate that about 2.5% of Brazil’s domestic gasoline consumption depends on Russian imports, while almost 12% of its diesel needs are supplied by Russia (Figure 3). These imports are distributed throughout the year, with a slightly higher concentration in the second half (Figure 4). In this context, we see the recent Russian export ban (along with ongoing capacity disruptions) as an additional source of pressure on global fuel supply. GS.excerpt: …risk of firmer data in September, as part of the long-haul component will only at that point start to reflect prices measured after the start of the Middle East conflict. On net, our estimates imply a slight rebound in services inflation over the rest of the year, before the slowing underlying trend results in a gradual deceleration in 2027. More Core Goods Pressure Ahead The incoming core goods inflation data has been mixed. The numbers surprised to the downside at the start of the conflict. But the seasonally adjusted sequential pace has been firmer at the last two prints, with strength in household goods and electronics prices. To assess the outlook, we combine two approaches. LLC Ecuador: Shrimp Exports Topped US$1bn and Supported the Trade Balance in July 11 September 2026 | 9:30AM EDT Bottom Line: Ecuador’s trade balance registered a US$504mn surplus in July. The reading compares to the US$203mn surplus in June and a US$256mn deficit posted a year ago. Exports were up 48.5% from a year ago, boosted by a favorable base effect (crude oil exports were up 332.8% yoy due to last year’s pipeline shutdown) as well as very strong shrimp exports (+64.4% yoy). Imports rose by 16.5% with fuel imports rising 35.4% yoy. Sizeable shrimp exports, due to warmer water conditions, boosted the trade balance in July. Shrimp exports topped US$1bn in a single month for the first time. The still high fuel imports, in turn, dragged the trade balance with the energy balance posting a US$58mn deficit in the month. JPM.title: US: Raising 3Q GDP to 2.75% despite wider trade deficit
JPM.excerpt: …JPMorgan Chase Bank NA The advance economic indicators showed an unexpected widening in the trade deficit in July, though with some offset from robust growth in nominal inventories. The goods deficit widened $17.4bn, as exports fell 2.9%m/m and imports rose 3.7%. The import rise was driven entirely by capital goods, and the capital goods deficit widened $12.3bn, which is good for domestic equipment investment. The drop in exports was driven by industrial supplies, which include petroleum, and excluding industrial supplies exports rose 2.4%. Meanwhile, total business inventories rose 0.8% in July. Nominal inventories have been rising briskly this year, though over the first half of the year that had still translated into a drop in real inventories. Taking stock of this and other data this week, which has included July PCE and durables, we’ve raised 3Q GDP tracking from 2.5% to 2.75%. While we’ve added half a percentage point to the trade drag and slightly lowered residential investment, that was offset by stronger consumer spending, which we’ve increased from 1.75% to 2.75%, and equipment, which we’ve raised from 10% to 12%. -175 -150 -125 -100 -75 -50 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 $bn, sa; Customs definiti…

Subcomponents were strong with new orders stable at 56.7, production rising sharply to 58.5, and employment finally moving above 50.0 to 52.8. The prices index remains elevated at 71.1, but has declined from its recent high of 84.6 reached when oil prices first rose in April. Citi’s Take – After sitting around 50.0 from 2023-2025, ISM manufacturing has moved more solidly into expansionary territory in 2026 and reached a multi-year high in July. Anecdotes from the survey suggest that much of the uptick in manufacturing activity can be traced back to the tail-wind from AI-investment with the need to build data centers and fill them with electronic equipment. The ISM survey data align with hard data showing robust orders for manufactured goods associated with AI infrastructure. Macro-Data Assessment Platform (MAP) GS MAP scores facilitate rapid interpretation of new data releases for economic indicators worldwide. MAP summarizes the importance of a specific data release (i.e., its historical correlation with GDP) and the degree of surprise relative to the consensus forecast. The sign on the degree of surprise characterizes underperformance with a negative number and outperformance with a positive number. Each of these two components is ranked on a scale from 0 to 5, with the MAP score being the product of the two, i.e., from -25 to +25. For example, a MAP score of +20 (5;+4) would indicate that the data has a very high correlation to GDP (5) and that it came out well above consensus expectations (+4), for a total MAP value of +20. Macro-Data Assessment Platform (MAP) GS MAP scores facilitate rapid interpretation of new data releases for economic indicators worldwide. MAP summarizes the importance of a specific data release (i.e., its historical correlation with GDP) and the degree of surprise relative to the consensus forecast. The sign on the degree of surprise characterizes underperformance with a negative number and outperformance with a positive number. Each of these two components is ranked on a scale from 0 to 5, with the MAP score being the product of the two, i.e., from -25 to +25. That should help to support consumption, and can potentially increase labour supply. Conventional estimates assume a labour supply elasticity to a 1% change in income, though effects vary across income groups. But the increase in social contributions via the pension reform and cuts to health care benefits may counter some of that impact. • Pension reform: the top-up of the public pay-as-you-go pension scheme with a capital-backed arm is a flagship element of the reform proposal. JPM.title: Canada: Solid June jobs report won’t jolt BoC
JPM.excerpt: …J P M O R G A N www.jpmorganmarkets.com Economic and Policy Research Michael S Hanson (1-212) 622-8603 [email omitted] Bennett Parrish (1-212) 622-9003 [email omitted] JPMorgan Chase Bank NA • Employment rose a further 18.2k in June after surging 87.8k in May • Job gains were largely confined to a 17.5k rise in part-time workers • The unemployment rate eased a tenth to 6.5%, down 0.4% since April • Wage growth firmed slightly, we don't see this report as convincing the BoC to pivot in the hawkish direction still priced by markets The June Labour Force Survey delivered a relatively solid follow-up to May’s remarkably strong report. One risk for industrial production (and thus GDP) are extremely low Rhine water levels, complicating transport via this important route. On 28 July, the level in Kaub dropped to just 28cm, the lowest since the dry and hot summer of 2018. One risk for industrial production (and thus GDP) are extremely low Rhine water levels, complicating transport via this important route. On 28 July, the level in Kaub dropped to just 28cm, the lowest since the dry and hot summer of 2018. Already at 40-50cm, vessels can only carry around 20% of their normal cargo, hence sharply reducing their transport capacity according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration. Our point is that the difference in ‘real economy’ price pressures between Canada and the US is not nearly as big as suggested by the core inflation indices. And this will be why consumer inflation expectations aren’t reflecting as large of a divergence. Price increases of the things that affect consumers and their confidence day-to-day – clothing, food, gasoline, furnishings – are not (on aggregate) much greater in one economy compared to the other. Regardless of this, the Fed will continue to monitor PCE and core PCE inflation (at least while the Fed’s task forces are underway) and Bank of Canada will continue to monitor its suite of underlying indicators in determining their respective policy rate paths – even if those measures have substantial differences. Differences in inflation measurement and focus may also be playing a role in why markets up until this point have priced in smaller near-term rate hikes from the Bank of Canada.

Core domestic private machinery orders fell 3.7%m/m sa in July, better than our expectation of a 5.5% decline. The pullback after June’s 9.7% increase was relatively modest and largely reflects still-solid demand from manufacturers. Manufacturers’ orders declined only 1.0%m/m sa after surging 19.9% in June, when large, AI-related orders boosted the headline. This pattern suggests that capex demand tied to AI-related areas, including material sectors, remains firm at the start of 3Q26. By contrast, core orders from non-manufacturers were softer, down 2.6%m/m sa. We still think non-manufacturers’ capex appetite remains supported by structural labor shortages, but higher input costs may be weighing on machinery orders and contributing to the recent pause. Machinery orders have not tracked GDP business capex well this year, even as the GDP data imply two consecutive quarters of contraction in business capex growth. Core domestic private machinery orders fell 12.4%m/m sa in May, much weaker than we expected. After a strong run from late last year through April, the May print likely reflects trend normalization, with orders down 8.3%3m/3m saar. The decline was also amplified by a reversal of April’s temporary surge, which had been driven by shipbuilding and transportation-related demand. Even allowing for some rebound in June, we now track machinery orders as contracting through 2Q. That said, the weakness follows two quarters of nearly 30%ar growth, and with business sentiment steady, we maintain our forecast of 2Q GDP business capex to rise 2.0%q/q saar, rebounding from the 1Q contraction. Within the details, manufacturing orders declined 14.9%m/m sa, largely due to an 80.5% drop in shipbuilding orders, which appears to be payback after temporary large-scale orders in April. One risk for industrial production (and thus GDP) are extremely low Rhine water levels, complicating transport via this important route. On 28 July, the level in Kaub dropped to just 28cm, the lowest since the dry and hot summer of 2018. Already at 40-50cm, vessels can only carry around 20% of their normal cargo, hence sharply reducing their transport capacity according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration. One risk for industrial production (and thus GDP) are extremely low Rhine water levels, complicating transport via this important route. On 28 July, the level in Kaub dropped to just 28cm, the lowest since the dry and hot summer of 2018. Already at 40-50cm, vessels can only carry around 20% of their normal cargo, hence sharply reducing their transport capacity according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration. Side effects are higher transport costs and potential disruptions of raw material supplies, as the Rhine is an important transport route for iron ore, coal, chemicals, petroleum products and other commodities. One risk for industrial production (and thus GDP) are extremely low Rhine water levels, complicating transport via this important route. On 28 July, the level in Kaub dropped to just 28cm, the lowest since the dry and hot summer of 2018. Already at 40-50cm, vessels can only carry around 20% of their normal cargo, hence sharply reducing their transport capacity according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration. Even more worrying, the weekly Bundesbank leading indicator fell off a cliff in the past few weeks, casting doubts upon a continued recovery (chart 4). One risk for industrial production (and thus GDP) are extremely low Rhine water levels, complicating transport via this important route. On 28 July, the level in Kaub dropped to just 28cm, the lowest since the dry and hot summer of 2018. Already at 40-50cm, vessels can only carry around 20% of their normal cargo, hence sharply reducing their transport capacity according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration. Side effects are higher transport costs and potential disruptions of raw material supplies, as the Rhine is an important transport route for iron ore, coal, chemicals, petroleum products and other commodities. Even more worrying, the weekly Bundesbank leading indicator fell off a cliff in the past few weeks, casting doubts upon a continued recovery (chart 4). One risk for industrial production (and thus GDP) are extremely low Rhine water levels, complicating transport via this important route. On 28 July, the level in Kaub dropped to just 28cm, the lowest since the dry and hot summer of 2018. Already at 40-50cm, vessels can only carry around 20% of their normal cargo, hence sharply reducing their transport capacity according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration. Side effects are higher transport costs and potential disruptions of raw material supplies, as the Rhine is an important transport route for iron ore, coal, chemicals, petroleum products and other commodities. The equilibrium policy rate—the rate at which the economy is in balance with inflation at target, often called r*—is back in focus, as some ECB officials have argued that monetary policy should turn mildly restrictive. The equilibrium rate is unobserved and very difficult to measure, but potentially an important input into monetary policymaking. The ECB staff estimated in early 2024 that the equilibrium rate had risen since the pre-Covid period, with the nominal neutral rate rising into a 1.75-2.25% range. ECB officials have recently suggested that the upper end of this range might have drifted up to 2.5%, with some Council members suggesting that r* could be even higher than that. The next three mandates coming to term are those of Chief Economist Lane (May 2027), President Lagarde (October 2027) and Schnabel, responsible for market operations (December 27). National central bank governors are appointed according to varying national procedures. How can 27 Governing Council members come to a decision? In theory, the Governing Council follows a voting rotation: the six Executive Board members vote at all times, the national central bank governors of the five largest members share four voting rights, and all the others share 11 voting rights, with a monthly rotation. We would refrain from spending much time on the rotation schedule. It’s a technical detail, with no tangible implication for policy outcomes, in our view. Citi.excerpt: US Economics 10 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Data – PPI final demand rose 0.4%MoM as expected in August. PPI excluding food and energy prices rose 0.2% while the core measure of PPI that also excludes trade services rose 0.3%. As a result of this “lock-in” effect, we expect existing home sales to total just 4.2mn in 2026, 22% below 2019 levels but a touch above the pace of the last two years. Next year, we expect existing home sales to edge up to roughly 4.3mn, reflecting both modestly lower mortgage rates and the natural decay of the lock-in effect that comes from, for example, borrowers paying down their mortgage. While a modest rebound in the pace of existing home sales would boost the gross supply of available homes, it would have limited implications for net housing supply and the longstanding—but moderating, as discussed below—nationwide housing shortage, as households are often simply switching between housing units and no housing units are created or destroyed. Citi.title: US Economics: Softer trend of new home sales as rates rise
Citi.excerpt: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 24 Jul 2026 11:07:02 ET │ 8 pages US Economics Softer trend of new home sales as rates rise CITI'S TAKE New home sales rose to 628k in June from an upwardly revised 618k in May, but the trend of new home sales is still clearly softer in 2026 compared to last year. This likely reflects new headwinds to demand from higher mortgage rates, as new home sales will be a timelier indicator of the impact of rates on housing. As higher rates weigh on demand, support for new home sales has come through modest declines in prices over the last three years. Supply of new homes for sale also remains elevated, suggesting downward pressure on prices can continue. With median prices of new and existing homes now at similar levels, further declines in new home prices could also weigh on existing home prices. As such, we expect shelter inflation to remain modest throughout this year and into 2027. As a result of this “lock-in” effect, we expect existing home sales to total just 4.2mn in 2026, 22% below 2019 levels but a touch above the pace of the last two years. Next year, we expect existing home sales to edge up to roughly 4.3mn, reflecting both modestly lower mortgage rates and the natural decay of the lock-in effect that comes from, for example, borrowers paying down their mortgage. While a modest rebound in the pace of existing home sales would boost the gross supply of available homes, it would have limited implications for net housing supply and the longstanding—but moderating, as discussed below—nationwide housing shortage, as households are often simply switching between housing units and no housing units are created or destroyed. Citi.title: US Economics: Softer trend of new home sales as rates rise
Citi.excerpt: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 24 Jul 2026 11:07:02 ET │ 8 pages US Economics Softer trend of new home sales as rates rise CITI'S TAKE New home sales rose to 628k in June from an upwardly revised 618k in May, but the trend of new home sales is still clearly softer in 2026 compared to last year. This likely reflects new headwinds to demand from higher mortgage rates, as new home sales will be a timelier indicator of the impact of rates on housing. As higher rates weigh on demand, support for new home sales has come through modest declines in prices over the last three years. Supply of new homes for sale also remains elevated, suggesting downward pressure on prices can continue. With median prices of new and existing homes now at similar levels, further declines in new home prices could also weigh on existing home prices. As such, we expect shelter inflation to remain modest throughout this year and into 2027. GS.title: US Daily: Lowering Our Q2 GDP Growth Forecast
GS.excerpt: While we often turn to domestic final sales (DFS)—which exclude the noisy trade and inventory components of the GDP statistics—as a better measure of underlying growth, there are two (partly offsetting) distortions impacting domestic final sales growth in Q2. First, while changes in private inventories are excluded from DFS, changes in the SPR are included via the federal government spending component and are not offset by changes in net exports in DFS, which weighs on DFS growth relative to GDP. Second (and not specific to just Q2), AI-related investment is sharply boosting business fixed investment, which is included in DFS. However, most of the value of AI investment is imported and therefore subtracted from GDP—an offset that is excluded from DFS. Ronnie Walker Jessica Rindels 29 July 2026 4 Goldman Sachs US Daily

The April MPR has real GDP growth in 2026Q2 as 0.7% under all scenarios. Scenario C growth diverges from the other two in 2026Q3, and only materially in Q4. Inasmuch as we would expect the MPC to converge on a view, it is unlikely to be in July as the May data broadly support MPCs' priors irrespective of which scenario they adhered to ex-ante. On the one hand, resilient services will be interpreted as supportive evidence that the economy is not contracting --- and it is the arm that powers the economy. Romania: NBR on Hold, Reflecting Inflation Risks The Board of the National Bank of Romania (NBR) will meet on Monday, August 10, and we expect it to keep its policy rate on hold at +6.50%, in line with consensus expectations. The NBR held rates unchanged at its July MPC meeting, indicating that the on hold decision was due to rising inflation and heightened uncertainties. Since then, headline inflation declined from +10.9%yoy to +10.4%yoy in June, and we expect inflation to fall further to +8.0%yoy in July on favourable base effects (see our preview below). Despite the steep correction expected from Q3 onwards, the NBR sees high risks to the medium-term inflation outlook. Accordingly, the NBR is likely to continue messaging caution and remain on hold until at least 2027Q1. In the case of hydrolyzed ethanol, the government announced a decrease of taxes of BRL0.19/liter, which would decrease consumer prices by ~5%, with an impact of - 3bps to headline CPI. In contrast, OER inflation in Canada is already sat around 0% year-on-year, and has limited room for further downside (even in 2009, after more than 400bps of easing and a property price decline, the component only took 0.2ppts off core inflation). This means that going into 2027, Canadian core inflation has more room to rise, peaking around April, then coming back down (our forecasts have peak core above 2.5%). Citi.excerpt: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 14 Aug 2026 11:25:19 ET │ 9 pages US Economics U Mich sentiment falls on business conditions CITI'S TAKE University of Michigan consumer sentiment unexpectedly fell to 51.0 in preliminary August data, with a decline in both current conditions and expectations indices. The decline was mostly due to an expectation of weaker business conditions. Inflation expectations were little changed and remain a bit lower than earlier in the year when gas prices first increased, and much lower than last year during tariff developments. The share of consumers saying it is a bad time to buy household goods because times are bad remains higher than last year, further evidence that the ability of businesses to pass on higher input costs to final selling prices is limited. Japan’s May industrial production rose 0.5%m/m sa, marking a second consecutive monthly increase but coming in below expectations (JPM: 1.0%; consensus: 1.1%). After strong gains through 1Q, output is still up 0.7%3m/3m saar. Producers have also turned more upbeat on the outlook: METI’s estimate implies a 2.6%m/m sa increase in June, and manufacturers anticipate output stabilizing in July at an elevated level. If these projections materialize, they would indicate that 2Q output growth remained solid following the 10.3%q/q saar expansion in 1Q, with momentum carrying into early 3Q. The key wildcard is inventories. Inventories fell for a third straight month in May, down 0.6%m/m sa. The tech sector is facing capacity constraints amid a global AI boom, and with supply frictions lingering after the energy price shocks, firms appear to have drawn down inventories to sustain production—particularly in autos, chemicals, and plastics. Citi.title: China Economics: Looking Through the August Numbers to Focus on Policies and Geopolitics
Citi.excerpt: …China Economics Looking Through the August Numbers to Focus on Policies and Geopolitics CITI'S TAKE China's economic momentum remained soft in August while the K-shaped divergence deepened. The supply side outperformed. Industrial production beat expectations on tech and exports. Domestic demand disappointed again with unexpected slowdown in retail sales and continuous weak fixed asset investment. Despite the dull picture, we see limited pressure on headline growth and maintain our forecasts at 4.5%YoY for 26Q3E and 4.6%YoY for the whole year. September indicators are key to deciding whether the economy finds a bottom within this year. Markets could look through this set of indicators to focus on a packaged policy and geopolitical agenda ahead. We continue to see rising risks of no LPR cuts this year should fiscal push come through, and expect the US-China tariff “truce” to hold through the upcoming Presidential Summit. Industrial production (IP) beat expectations, with growth accelerating to 5.2% yoy in August from 4.5% yoy in July amid stronger exports and faster output growth in the electric machinery, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals industries. FAI contracted 10.8% yoy in August on a single-month basis, although favorable base effects narrowed the decline from -12.8% yoy in July. GS.title: China Matters: Path of Least Resistance
GS.excerpt: Path of Least Resistance The Gap Keeps Growing China’s August activity data showed a widening divergence between supply and demand, and between manufacturing output and household consumption. Industrial production growth accelerated from 4.5% yoy in July to 5.2% in August, while retail sales growth slowed from 0.6% yoy to 0.4%. Among major activity indicators, only export value and industrial production growth exceeded 5.0% yoy in August. By contrast, many domestic demand gauges continued to post large year-over-year declines (Exhibit 1). For exports, we can cross-check the data against trading partners’ reported imports from China. Such “mirror data” support strong Chinese export growth. For domestic demand, however, there are statistical reasons why official data may understate the true weakness. For example, in retail sales, large retailers above the designated size are surveyed comprehensively, whereas small retailers are sampled and estimated because of their large numbers and the difficulty of surveying every small retailer each month (see our latest edition of “Understanding China’s Economic Statistics” for more details). Citi.title: China Economics: Looking Through the August Numbers to Focus on Policies and Geopolitics
Citi.excerpt: …China Economics Looking Through the August Numbers to Focus on Policies and Geopolitics CITI'S TAKE China's economic momentum remained soft in August while the K-shaped divergence deepened. The supply side outperformed. Industrial production beat expectations on tech and exports. Domestic demand disappointed again with unexpected slowdown in retail sales and continuous weak fixed asset investment. Despite the dull picture, we see limited pressure on headline growth and maintain our forecasts at 4.5%YoY for 26Q3E and 4.6%YoY for the whole year. September indicators are key to deciding whether the economy finds a bottom within this year. Markets could look through this set of indicators to focus on a packaged policy and geopolitical agenda ahead. We continue to see rising risks of no LPR cuts this year should fiscal push come through, and expect the US-China tariff “truce” to hold through the upcoming Presidential Summit. We would argue that while this is all true, it’s not so much how high prices went, in as much as that they did move, and now they are not. • How can we signal whether or not wages growth may start to pick up? The headline wage growth data from the DMP will show that it is moderating. This would be somewhere in between the baseline (2.3%) and adverse scenario (3.0%) in the June Projections. This up-revision to 2027 inflation would be driven by higher gas prices feeding through slowly from Aug-26, slightly higher unit labour costs and possibly larger second-round effects from energy. The rebound in food price inflation expected in June will likely remain a feature of the forecasts (despite recent weakness). The inflation ‘hump’ will therefore look a bit higher and more stretched out than in the June Projections. We still expect the 2028 HICP forecast to remain close to 2.0% (with a possibility for it to move to 2.1% instead of 2.0%). Prepared for Jeyhyuk Im

The boost to activity in Q2 from increased oil exports and production will likely also slow in future quarters. In our base case, growth is still averaging below potential – even with a 3.3% increase in Q2 and upward revisions, quarterly GDP growth has averaged 1.1% since Q1-2025. Core domestic private machinery orders made a strong start to 2Q, following robust growth in 1Q. Orders rose 8.7%m/m sa in April, suggesting that the strong momentum seen in 4Q25 and 1Q26—running close to 30%q/q saar—has continued into 2Q. The details suggest that the strength in orders is beginning to broaden. In 2025, strength in orders was driven mainly by non-manufacturing, while momentum in manufacturing was relatively less robust. More recently, however, manufacturing orders have begun to catch up. In fact, in April both non- manufacturing and manufacturing posted balanced growth in orders, at 6.7%m/m sa and 5.1%, respectively. Citi.title: US Economics: Housing activity to weaken further
Citi.excerpt: …view – Housing starts have softened in recent months and will likely pull back further as higher rates weigh on housing demand. Recent high frequency data have already showed a renewed slowing in housing activity, with mortgage applications now falling on an annual basis for the first time since late 2024. We expect residential investment to continue to weigh on GDP growth in coming quarters. Weakness in housing starts in July was concentrated in single family starts, which bounced-back in August. This bounce-back is not surprising given that starts were much weaker than building permits. But as construction spending tends to correlate with a trend of housing starts, softer single family starts over the last few months could imply another decline in single family residential construction spending. Construction spending is a direct input into residential investment in GDP. But going forward, we would expect further slowing in both starts and permits, with single family building permits falling modestly in August.
